result.builder:
Goal: add a --tsv flag to the CLI so it reads tab-separated input. Make one pull request that meets every acceptance line below.

Current state (read these first):
- bin/csv2json.js reads stdin and calls parse(readFileSync(0, 'utf8')) with no separator. It ignores all arguments.
- src/parse.js exports parse(text, sep = ','). Splitting on the separator is naive, and you can reuse this parameter.
- test/csv.test.js uses node:test and has a 'cli' test that runs execFileSync('node', ['bin/csv2json.js'], { input, encoding: 'utf8' }). npm test runs `node --test`.
- README.md shows only `node bin/csv2json.js < table.csv`.

Steps:
1. In bin/csv2json.js, check whether process.argv.slice(2) includes '--tsv'. The flag may appear anywhere among the arguments. If it is there, call parse(text, '	'). If not, call parse(text) exactly as today. Keep the output format unchanged: JSON.stringify(...) followed by a single '
'. Do not change how unknown arguments are handled, add --help, add a general --sep/--delimiter option, auto-detect the separator, or add quoting rules.
2. Leave src/parse.js alone unless you really need to change it. If you do change it, its behaviour without the flag must stay the same.
3. In test/ (for example test/csv.test.js), add at least one node:test test that runs bin/csv2json.js with the '--tsv' argument on tab-separated input through execFileSync and asserts the exact output. Suggested cases: 'a	b
1	2
' -> '[{"a":"1","b":"2"}]
'; 'name	note
x	hello, world
' -> '[{"name":"x","note":"hello, world"}]
'; 'a	b
1	2
3	4
' -> '[{"a":"1","b":"2"},{"a":"3","b":"4"}]
'. Also add a test that tab input without the flag still gives '[{"a\tb":"1\t2"}]
' (the JSON tab escape). Keep the existing tests.
4. In README.md, document the --tsv flag with an example invocation such as `node bin/csv2json.js --tsv < table.tsv`, and say that it reads tab-separated input. Keep the CSV example.
5. Run npm test and each of the commands below, and confirm the results.

Acceptance lines (all must hold):
- `printf 'a	b
1	2
' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv` prints exactly `[{"a":"1","b":"2"}]` followed by a newline and exits 0.
- With --tsv, commas inside a field stay literal: `printf 'name	note
x	hello, world
' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv` prints exactly `[{"name":"x","note":"hello, world"}]` followed by a newline.
- With --tsv and several data rows, every row comes out in order: `printf 'a	b
1	2
3	4
' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv` prints exactly `[{"a":"1","b":"2"},{"a":"3","b":"4"}]` followed by a newline.
- Without the flag, CSV still works as before: `printf 'a,b
1,2
' | node bin/csv2json.js` prints exactly `[{"a":"1","b":"2"}]` followed by a newline.
- Without the flag, tabs are not treated as separators: `printf 'a	b
1	2
' | node bin/csv2json.js` prints exactly `[{"a	b":"1	2"}]` followed by a newline, which is the current output.
- `npm test` exits 0, and test/ contains at least one test that runs bin/csv2json.js with --tsv on tab-separated input and checks its output.
- README.md documents the --tsv flag with an example invocation.
result.verifier:
Check the PR head from the repository root. Run each command exactly as written. There is one check per acceptance line, in order. Each output comparison uses cmp against the expected bytes, so a missing or extra newline counts as a mismatch.

Check 1. Expect line: `printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv` prints exactly `[{"a":"1","b":"2"}]` followed by a newline and exits 0.
Run:
printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv > /tmp/v1.out; echo "exit=$?"; printf '[{"a":"1","b":"2"}]\n' | cmp - /tmp/v1.out && echo MATCH
PASS: the output shows exit=0 and MATCH. FAIL: any other exit code, or cmp reports a difference.

Check 2. Expect line: With --tsv, commas inside a field stay literal: `printf 'name\tnote\nx\thello, world\n' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv` prints exactly `[{"name":"x","note":"hello, world"}]` followed by a newline.
Run:
printf 'name\tnote\nx\thello, world\n' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv > /tmp/v2.out; echo "exit=$?"; printf '[{"name":"x","note":"hello, world"}]\n' | cmp - /tmp/v2.out && echo MATCH
PASS: MATCH is printed. FAIL: cmp reports a difference.

Check 3. Expect line: With --tsv and several data rows, every row comes out in order: `printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n3\t4\n' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv` prints exactly `[{"a":"1","b":"2"},{"a":"3","b":"4"}]` followed by a newline.
Run:
printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n3\t4\n' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv > /tmp/v3.out; echo "exit=$?"; printf '[{"a":"1","b":"2"},{"a":"3","b":"4"}]\n' | cmp - /tmp/v3.out && echo MATCH
PASS: MATCH is printed. FAIL: cmp reports a difference.

Check 4. Expect line: Without the flag, CSV still works as before: `printf 'a,b\n1,2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js` prints exactly `[{"a":"1","b":"2"}]` followed by a newline.
Run:
printf 'a,b\n1,2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js > /tmp/v4.out; echo "exit=$?"; printf '[{"a":"1","b":"2"}]\n' | cmp - /tmp/v4.out && echo MATCH
PASS: MATCH is printed. FAIL: cmp reports a difference.

Check 5. Expect line: Without the flag, tabs are not treated as separators: `printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js` prints exactly `[{"a\tb":"1\t2"}]` followed by a newline, which is the current output.
Run:
printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js > /tmp/v5.out; echo "exit=$?"; printf '[{"a\\tb":"1\\t2"}]\n' | cmp - /tmp/v5.out && echo MATCH
(The expected bytes use the JSON escape, a backslash followed by t, not a real tab.) PASS: MATCH is printed. FAIL: cmp reports a difference.

Check 6. Expect line: `npm test` exits 0, and test/ contains at least one test that runs bin/csv2json.js with --tsv on tab-separated input and checks its output.
Run:
npm test; echo "exit=$?"
grep -n -- '--tsv' test/*.js
Then read each matching test.
PASS: the first command shows exit=0, and at least one test in test/ runs bin/csv2json.js with the --tsv argument on input that contains tab characters and asserts on its output. FAIL: npm test exits non-zero, or no such test exists (for example, a match that is only a comment, or a test that never checks the CLI output).

Check 7. Expect line: README.md documents the --tsv flag with an example invocation.
Run:
grep -n -- '--tsv' README.md
Then read README.md.
PASS: README.md documents the --tsv flag and includes an example command line that uses it (for example `node bin/csv2json.js --tsv < table.tsv`). FAIL: the flag is not mentioned, or it is mentioned with no example invocation.

Advisory (does not affect PASS/FAIL):
- Scope: the issue's non-goals are quoting rules, a general --sep option, auto-detection, changes to unknown-argument handling or --help, and changes to JSON formatting. Note any of these if the diff adds them.
- You could also check that the flag works when it is not the first argument, e.g. `printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js foo --tsv`.
